newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait Central Bank curbs securities trade loans.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait Central Bank curbs securities trade loans.

text.p: Kuwait's Central Bank ordered local banks to stop extending margin loans and to diversify guarantees required against lending for securities trading, the official Kuwait News Agency reported on Sunday.

"The new directives stipulate that a timetable should be put to settle the balances of debts from these facilities in a gradual manner that secures their full repayment on maturity dates," it quoted Central Bank Governor Sheikh Salem Abdul-Aziz al-Sabah as saying.
The measure is apparently designed to reduce liquidity on the Kuwait Stock Exchange (KSE) whose index has risen 25 percent since the start of 1997 compared to 40 percent in all of 1996.

Loans for securities trading "amounted to 425 million dinars ($1.407 billion) of which 96 million dinars were margin loans," he said of the figure, that overshot independent estimates by about 100 million dinars.

"Banks should reduce their credit balance extended for securities trading by about 130 million dinars within the coming seven months," he said. The 130 million figure represented 10 percent of the credit extended to resident clients at the date the bank's directives were drafted, Sheikh Salem said.

Sheikh Salem in May held a meeting with Kuwait's top bankers to discuss ways of stabilising the KSE which has registered successive peaks since the start of 1997, triggering fears among some economists of a crash.
"A maximum limit has been put for those facilities so that they do not exceed 10 percent of total credit extended to resident clients or 25 percent of any bank's capital," he said.

In late April, trading value on the KSE soared to 125.8 million dinars during a single 2-1/2-hour session. In the week to Wednesday daily average for value of traded shares rose to 76.6 million dinars from 39 million in the previous week.
Banks were required to cut their credit portfolios by the end of 1997 to match the target set by the Central Bank and to provide the Bank with a timetable for doing so, he said.
The Central Bank's orders also oblige banks to guarantee that their clients would not use credit for purposes other than those it was allocated for.
Kuwait has six commercial banks, two specialised banks, an Islamic finance institution and a branch of a Bahrain-based bank.
